props.title: The Devil's Brigade
props.initialSlug: Elite misfits unite to become WWII's deadliest unit

sections.content: The Devil's Brigade (1968) stands as a gritty WWII combat film that helped bridge the gap between classical 1950s war movies and the grittier late 1960s takes. Following the true story of the First Special Service Force, it stars William Holden leading a mixed unit of Canadian and American troops. The film shares DNA with The Dirty Dozen (1967), released just a year earlier, in its focus on misfit soldiers molded into an elite fighting force. Both films influenced later special forces movies like Force 10 from Navarone (1978) and Inglourious Basterds (2009).

sections.content: What sets The Devil's Brigade apart is its basis in historical fact. The actual First Special Service Force was a pioneering special operations unit that helped establish modern special forces tactics. The film captures their intensive training and dangerous missions, particularly the crucial assault on Mount la Difensa. This historical grounding puts it in company with other fact-based WWII films like The Great Escape (1963) and A Bridge Too Far (1977), though it takes more dramatic liberties than those productions.

The film's depiction of Canadian-American cooperation was groundbreaking for its time, predating later allied force narratives like Battle of Britain (1969) and A Bridge Too Far (1977). Director Andrew V. McLaglen, known for westerns like McLintock! (1963), brings a rugged sensibility to the combat sequences that influenced later war films like Where Eagles Dare (1968) and The Guns of Navarone (1961). SUBHEAD: Impact on Special Forces Cinema

sections.content: The Devil's Brigade helped establish many tropes of special forces movies: the intensive training sequence, the clash between different military cultures, and the seemingly impossible mission. These elements echo through later films like Who Dares Wins (1982), Navy SEALs (1990), and even modern interpretations like Act of Valor (2012). The film's influence can be seen in its realistic portrayal of special operations tactics, which was ahead of its time.
